title: Stoicism: A Philosophy for Idiots
summary: First episode of a 'Philosophy for Idiots' series. NH credits Stoicism for being accessible and practical, especially for men, but argues it was built to temper the passionate Greeks and Romans and becomes passivity for modern, under-aggressive men. Online 'pathological stoicism' suppresses emotions, reduces the philosophy to quotes and turns readers into dogmatic men of one book.
claims: Every philosophy can improve our lives; the series aims to show limits and help people use ideas more healthily, not to call some philosophies bad
Stoicism is the most popular philosophy online because it focuses on self-improvement, which appeals mainly to men; its audience is about 95-97% male
Calling Stoicism a philosophy for idiots isn't purely negative: it's accessible and needs no background, unlike Nietzsche or continental philosophy
Using hard philosophy as a status symbol is misusing philosophy to feel superior rather than to become better
Stoicism is popular because it is directly applicable advice, which answers the main criticism that philosophy is useless
For men, Stoicism is the most effective form of therapy: men need a list of actionable items
The ancients didn't build Stoicism because they were calm but because they were passionate and Dionysian; it was an Apollonian structure to temper their chaos
Maxims like 'nothing in excess' and 'know thyself' show the Greeks needed to be reminded of moderation
Greek statues had small penises to encourage sexual self-control, while modern porn worships the opposite to push men toward animal consumerism
Temperance still helps resist hedonism and consumerism, but the average modern male lacks aggressive energy, so tempering nothing breeds passivity
Righteous anger is important today; the line between controlling emotions and being a coward is very thin
He resonates more with Bushido, which puts honour and protecting others above self-preservation
Modern Stoicism treats emotions as obstacles to suppress, but Marcus Aurelius and Seneca acknowledged emotions as part of virtue
To master your emotions you must first understand and accept them; rejecting them means you aren't even working with the material Stoicism needs
'Facts over feelings' is an empty slogan from people caricaturing masculinity
Suppressed feelings resurface; Jung held that ignoring or destroying feelings that take over your life destroys you
'Pathological stoicism' is the compulsive rejection of all feelings for a fake stability; it brings back anxiety, depression and low confidence
Stoicism is first a practice: Marcus wrote the Meditations as daily reminders; it only takes root when it becomes daily habits
Instagram quote pages teach what to think rather than how to think; vulgarising complex ideas leaves almost no chance of real application
Read the primary texts: the Meditations, Epictetus and Seneca's On the Happy Life cost about $9 and take two weeks
Many men start and stop with Stoicism and become 'men of one book'
'Chase two rabbits, catch neither' applies to fitness, which rewards specialisation, but not to intellect: expose yourself to many schools of thought
Online Stoicism has become dogmatic, rejecting everything outside its texts; he wants wisdom, not partisanship
Nietzsche is a black hole that traps young readers; reading only one author's take on others is a 'will to stupidity'
Stoic assertions are subjective but presented as objective; treat the text as a guide and approach philosophy with irreverence
Nietzsche objected to Stoicism's claim to be natural; it was created to civilise people against their nature, so it is unnatural, which isn't a bad thing
Reject modernity's negative effects on you, not modernity itself; refusing the challenges of your time contradicts Stoicism
Marcus aimed at virtuous individuals for a virtuous society; hyper-individualist modern Stoicism became selfish self-improvement and needs a renewed, contextual version
